title: You Can’t Learn What You Can’t Connect
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: Drawing on Hector Ruiz Martin's How Do We Learn?, the author argues that learning is meaningful only when new information connects to prior knowledge in long-term memory. She contrasts a classroom where clear explanation produces inert knowledge, understood in the moment but not durable, with one where the teacher anchors a new idea in something familiar before explaining it. Analogies are presented as the tool that makes the connection deliberate, illustrated with three classroom examples from a wildfire unit: a grape turning into a raisin, a savings account for snowpack, and removing all stress for fire suppression. The closing claim is that exposure is not learning and clarity is not retention, so teachers should start from what students already know.
points: Clear explanation alone can produce inert knowledge, an illusion of learning that is neither durable nor usable.
Prior knowledge is one of the most powerful drivers of learning because it gives new ideas somewhere to attach.
Analogies work not by simplifying but by connecting the unfamiliar to existing schema, making learning more meaningful.
Three wildfire-unit examples (grape to raisin, savings account, no-stress homework) show the technique in practice.
Long-term memory is a network, so knowledge without a connection point has nowhere to go.
quotes: The first scenario produces what we might call inert knowledge which is information that can be understood in the moment, even repeated back, but never really becomes usable or lasting. It gives the illusion that learning has occurred, when in reality, nothing durable and usable has been built.

From a cognitive science perspective, learning becomes meaningful only when new information connects to prior knowledge in long-term memory. Without that connection, ideas remain abstract and isolated, making them difficult to retain and even harder to use and transfer.
Instead of asking students to build a new concept from scratch, I said, “Think about a grape turning into a raisin.” They immediately had something to work with.
Now they had a structure to think with. “Winter is when you build your savings. Spring and summer is when you spend it.
This is the real power of analogies. They don’t just simplify. They connect. They activate prior knowledge, align relationships, and allow new information to integrate into existing schema.
Long-term memory is not a blank slate or an empty library shelf to be filled up. It’s a network. New knowledge doesn’t get stored in isolation.
